Hardware engineer here. It is very hard to discern jack shit with him flailing the board around like a retard.

The shiny rectangle is an RF shield that is soldered to the board. It is soldered on over some other components which are sensitive to RF and/or may radiate RF, causing interference. The cylindrical protrusion near the RF shield looks like a coax connector, so this is plausibly an antenna connection. All this is consistent with the idea that what's under the RF shield is a radio interface.

As for the "COV-19" label, he could have easily laser-etched it himself by the same means that people get their name printed on a metallic phone or laptop. It sure looks "professional" don't it? Not to me.

It is unusual for manufactures to print things on the steel in that manner. This would add an extra process to the manufacturing. Normally, such labeling information is silk-screened or pad-printed onto the components or the PCB, or perhaps a sticky label. Not usually laser-etched into steel, and not usually in such conveniently huge typeface. I'm not saying it's inconceivable, I just haven't seen it much. Usually those steel can tops are blank.

The rest of the PCB contains what looks like a CPU and memory, and maybe the baseband stuff, obviously high speed stuff as you can tell by the panoply of very tiny decoupling caps and other passives on the back of the PCB.

The whole thing is not unlike what you might find in a consumer cable modem device. However there is a black connector about the size of a DB25 which is clearly not a common type of connector that you see on consumer gear. It may be for plugging into a backplane or something. At t=38 if you search for just the right still frame you can get a better view of this connector. It looks to have RF shielding. Don't know what it is.

Also on the front edge of the board there is possibly what looks like a 7-segment display and some other LEDs, so this leads me towards the idea that this is indeed a line card or whatever you call them.

In conclusion it is totally plausible that this is a card that goes in a modern cellular tower. But the COV-19 printing looks clumsy and contrived.

Here's what's wrong with the board. First of all, the basics: It's not the type of board that would go in a climate exposed tower. The type of board that goes in such locations has a conformal coating that protects all components from the weather and will protect it and keep it running even if it is fully immersed in water. It is the wrong circuit type.

Second problem: There are display LED's on the board, and for the type of application a tower would use, they'd be pointing up, not forward. This board is for a device that is visible from the front, and accessible from the back. If it was for a cell tower, any indicators and connectors would be at most 90 degrees different, not 180. Home electronics are 180 because you don't want to see the connectors, just the display. Pro electronics are not that way at all, you see both at once. That alone proves this is a consumer item and not anything that would be for commercial use.

Third problem: The RF output is for direct connection to another device, not an antenna. If it was for a transmitting antenna of the type needed for 5G, it would be accompanied by a circuit that had an ultra stabilizing heat sink that weighed at least 5 pounds.

4th problem: If it was only the processor board, it's not robust enough for the application. 5G is for moving an enormous pile of data to multiple people at once, and I don't think what looks like a 32 bit processor running megahertz would do that. In fact, I know it won't.

5th problem: There are only 3 board stand offs and no external ground planes going to the board. It's not supported well enough or grounded well enough to be stable enough for commercial use.

Most likely candidate for that particular board: A satellite box, early 2000's vintage. If that's not the case, 5G is pre planned to be so temporary and cheaply made that it won't have a life span more than six months. And the display pointing forward basically cinches it, even if 5G was being done cheap enough to skip the conformal coatings and other details the display would still face up, not forward.

CONCLUSION: IT IS NOT A 5G BOARD.
